meaning: to choose; a choice between options
core: 选择 is the common, neutral term for making a choice, used both as an action and as a noun for the available options themselves. Learners often overuse it in very casual contexts where 选 alone sounds more natural, or forget it works as a noun meaning the range of options a shop or service offers.

sentences.situation: At a restaurant · to your dining companion
sentences.zh: 菜单给你，你先选择想吃的菜。
sentences.pinyin: cài dān gěi nǐ, nǐ xiān xuǎn zé xiǎng chī de cài.
sentences.en: Here's the menu, you pick what you want to eat first.
sentences.why: Said to a friend or family member while dining out, it politely lets the other person take the lead ordering, no pressure to pick fancy dishes.
sentences.tip: Saying 选 instead of 选择 sounds even more casual between close friends.

sentences.situation: At a clothing store · to the shop assistant
sentences.zh: 你们店还有其他颜色可以选择吗？
sentences.pinyin: nǐ men diàn hái yǒu qí tā yán sè kě yǐ xuǎn zé ma?
sentences.en: Do you have other colors I can choose from in this shop?
sentences.why: Said to a retail clerk when browsing clothes or home goods, it asks about the available range of options without sounding pushy.
sentences.tip: This is a standard polite shopping line; you can swap 颜色 for 尺码, 款式 to ask about size or style options.

sentences.situation: At a job interview · to the hiring manager
sentences.zh: 我选择这份工作，是因为我很喜欢这个行业。
sentences.pinyin: wǒ xuǎn zé zhè fèn gōng zuò, shì yīn wèi wǒ hěn xǐ huān zhè ge háng yè.
sentences.en: I chose this job because I really love this industry.
sentences.why: A candidate explaining their motivation for applying, this frames their choice as deliberate and aligned with their career interests, impressing interviewers.
sentences.tip: Avoid sounding too casual here; 选择 comes across more thoughtful than the shorter 选 in an interview context.

sentences.situation: On a long road trip · to your family member in the car
sentences.zh: 中午吃饭，你想选择哪一家餐厅？
sentences.pinyin: zhōng wǔ chī fàn, nǐ xiǎng xuǎn zé nǎ yì jiā cān tīng?
sentences.en: Which restaurant do you want to pick for lunch?
sentences.why: Said to family members during travel, it invites input on meal plans to make sure everyone feels heard.
sentences.tip: Drop 选择 and just say 选 which restaurant for a more relaxed, natural vibe with people you know well.

sentences.situation: Talking to a close friend about their career plans
sentences.zh: 你已经拿到两个offer了，为什么还要选择继续读书？
sentences.pinyin: nǐ yǐ jīng ná dào liǎng gè offer le, wèi shén me hái yào xuǎn zé jì xù dú shū?
sentences.en: You already got two job offers, why are you still choosing to keep studying instead?
sentences.why: A close friend asking about a seemingly unexpected life choice, it shows they care about your decision and are curious about your reasoning, not judging you.
sentences.tip: Raise your tone on 为什么 to signal gentle curiosity rather than harsh criticism.

sentences.situation: WeChat message to your teammate before a project meeting
sentences.zh: 这次活动我们有两个方案可以选择，你更倾向哪一个？
sentences.pinyin: zhè cì huó dòng wǒ men yǒu liǎng gè fāng àn kě yǐ xuǎn zé, nǐ gèng qīng xiàng nǎ yí gè?
sentences.en: We have two possible plans to choose from for this event, which one do you lean toward?
sentences.why: A teammate messaging ahead of a meeting to align on options, it invites input before the discussion to save meeting time.
sentences.tip: This is a standard workplace written line; you can shorten 可以选择 to 可选 in quick internal chat messages.

sentences.situation: Talking to your younger cousin who is stressing over exam choices
sentences.zh: 别太焦虑，高考只是人生的选择之一，不是唯一的路。
sentences.pinyin: bié tài jiāo lǜ, gāo kǎo zhǐ shì rén shēng de xuǎn zé zhī yī, bú shì wéi yī de lù.
sentences.en: Don't be too anxious, the college entrance exam is just one of life's choices, not the only path.
sentences.why: An older relative comforting a stressed teen, it frames high-stakes exams as one option among many to reduce pressure, a very common sentiment in Chinese family conversations.
sentences.tip: Say 之一 slowly and gently to sound more comforting; rushing the line will sound dismissive.

sentences.situation: Talking to your friend after they made a regrettable impulsive purchase
sentences.zh: 既然已经买了，就不要再后悔自己的选择了。
sentences.pinyin: jì rán yǐ jīng mǎi le, jiù bú yào zài hòu huǐ zì jǐ de xuǎn zé le.
sentences.en: Since you already bought it, don't keep regretting your choice.
sentences.why: A friend helping another move past buyer's remorse, it encourages acceptance of a past decision instead of ruminating on what could have been.
sentences.tip: Use 既然 here to signal 'since it's already done' — this softens the advice so it doesn't sound preachy.

sentences.situation: On a work trip · talking to your colleague over coffee
sentences.zh: 其实我也没得选，当时公司就给我这一个选择，我只能过来。
sentences.pinyin: qí shí wǒ yě méi dé xuǎn, dāng shí gōng sī jiù gěi wǒ zhè yí gè xuǎn zé, wǒ zhǐ néng guò lái.
sentences.en: Honestly I had no choice, the company only gave me this one option back then, so I just had to come here.
sentences.why: A colleague venting about being assigned to an unwanted work location, using 没得选 to explain they had no real agency, which builds rapport with peers who share similar frustrations.
sentences.tip: The colloquial 没得选 is far more natural here than the formal 没有选择 when chatting with peers; don't use this line to your boss.

sentences.situation: WeChat reply to your friend who is overthinking takeout options
sentences.zh: 你别纠结了，要不就选上次那家吧，选择太多反而更难决定。
sentences.pinyin: nǐ bié jiū jié le, yào bù jiù xuǎn shàng cì nà jiā ba, xuǎn zé tài duō fǎn ér gèng nán jué dìng.
sentences.en: Stop overthinking, how about we just pick that place we got last time? Too many options actually make it harder to decide.
sentences.why: A friend teasing someone with well-known decision paralysis, it references the common experience of choice overload to push for a quick, low-fuss decision.
sentences.tip: Drop the tone on 吧 to sound friendly and not bossy; this is a super common line in Chinese friend chat about food plans.

quiz.prompt: You are at a restaurant with a friend. Hand them the menu and tell them they can pick what they want to eat first.
quiz.answer: 菜单给你，你先选择想吃的菜。
accept: 你先选想吃的菜吧，菜单给你。
菜单给你，你先选想吃什么。
quiz.explain: This is the natural casual line to cede ordering control to a dining companion, using 选择 to frame the action of picking dishes.

quiz.prompt: You are in a clothing store, politely ask the shop assistant if there are other colors you can choose from.
quiz.answer: 你们店还有其他颜色可以选择吗？
accept: 请问还有别的颜色可以选择吗？
这款还有其他颜色可以选吗？
quiz.explain: This is the standard polite shopping line to ask about available product options, using 选择 to refer to selectable variants.

quiz.prompt: You are in a job interview, sincerely explain to the hiring manager that you chose this job because you love this industry.
quiz.answer: 我选择这份工作，是因为我很喜欢这个行业。
accept: 我之所以选择这份工作，是因为我非常喜欢这个行业。
我选择这份工作，主要是因为我热爱这个行业。
quiz.explain: This formal, earnest line frames your career choice as deliberate and aligned with your interests, which is expected in interview settings.

quiz.prompt: Your younger cousin is panicking about taking the college entrance exam. Comfort them by saying the exam is just one of life's choices, not the only path.
quiz.answer: 别太焦虑，高考只是人生的选择之一，不是唯一的路。
accept: 别太担心，高考只是人生的选择之一，不是唯一的出路。
你别焦虑，高考只是人生众多选择里的一个，不是唯一的路。
quiz.explain: This comforting line reframes high-stakes exams as one option among many, a very common reassuring phrase for stressed students in Chinese families.

quiz.prompt: 你的朋友已经拿到两个工作offer，却还是选择继续读书。你很好奇他为什么这么选，用中文问他。
quiz.answer: 你都拿到两个offer了，为什么还要选择继续读书呀？
accept: 你已经有两个offer了，为什么还选择继续读书呢？
你都拿到两个工作offer了，怎么还选择继续读书啊？
quiz.explain: This natural curious question uses 选择 to reference the person's unexpected life decision, matching the gentle, concerned tone of a close friend asking about their plans.

quiz.prompt: 你的朋友一直在纠结点哪家外卖，选择太多拿不定主意。你劝他别纠结，就选上次那家，说选择太多反而更难决定。
quiz.answer: 你别纠结了，要不就选上次那家吧，选择太多反而更难决定。
accept: 你别纠结了，就选上次那家吧，选择太多反而更难选。
别纠结了，要不就点上次那家吧，选择太多反而更难决定。
quiz.explain: This playful, practical line references the common experience of choice overload, a very common casual phrase between friends deciding on takeout.
